name: Money changer (FXD/MC) BSP and AMLC compliance pack
buyer: Single-office BSP-registered money changers and small remittance agents (MSBs)
trigger: BSP MORNBFI Sec 901-N registration; AMLC Secretariat registration within 30 days and covered/suspicious transaction reporting; BSP draft M-Regulations (2024); registrations cancelled for AML violations (4 barred May 2025, 11 revoked since 2024)
evidence: https://business.inquirer.net/?p=223234 ; https://context.ph/2025/05/17/bsp-bars-four-firms-for-unauthorized-money-service-operations/ ; https://verihubs.com/ph/blog/money-service-business-philippines ; 7,357 registered MSBs end-2023 (secondary source); covered-transaction threshold PHP 500,000 per day (from a generic FI source, unverified for MSBs)
existing: Competitor search run: 247 RemitPlus by Mohur (2016, unclear if still sold); generic AML vendors (Tookitaki, enterprise). No small-MSB-specific tool found.
unchecked: Final status of M-Regulations/BSP Circular 1206 text; AMLC reporting channel and format for small MSBs; how many are standalone single-office changers vs. large remittance firms; existing POS vendors for forex counters; K07 pawnshop pack overlap in design but different buyer

first_check.duty: The duty is real and in force. BSP Circular No. 1206 (23 Dec 2024, Monetary Board Res. 1362) removed MORNBFI Secs 901-N and 902-N and replaced them with the M-Regulations. These cover remittance transfer companies, money changers and FX dealers. A second circular, reported as No. 1222 (MB approval 14 Aug 2025), amends the reporting rules in Secs 151-M to 154-M. Secondary summaries say it sets reporting standards, monetary and non-monetary sanctions, and audited financial statement deadlines. I could not open its full text (HTTP 429). Separately, the AML law (RA 9160, as amended by RA 11211) requires: (1) registration with the AMLC on portal.amlc.gov.ph; (2) covered transaction reports for cash over PHP 500,000 in one banking day, due within 5 working days; (3) suspicious transaction reports with no threshold, due the next working day after suspicion arises, filed through GoTRACS. The CTR and STR terms come from secondary sources only, not checked against AMLC text. Enforcement is real: MB cancelled Prince Rockwell, Kings Hopewell and World Reliance for persistent AMLA violations (CL-2025-028), barred 4 unregistered operators (CL-2025-021), and cancelled sole proprietorships (Edzen, World Wide Money Changer). Not verified: exact BSP report forms, how often they are due, and penalty amounts per day of delay.
first_check.market: The claim cites 7,357 registered MSBs at end-2023 (secondary source). Verihubs cites BSP data of about 5,300 head offices, 12,700 branches and 6,700 pawnshops holding MSB licences, but its totals do not add up. Likely buyers are a few thousand single-office changers and remittance agents. I did not find an official 2024 or 2025 count.
first_check.competitor: No product built for small Philippine money changers was found. Tookitaki sells enterprise AML (screening, monitoring, CTR/STR filing). Verihubs sells eKYC, watchlist screening and OCR APIs aimed at agent networks. Foreign bureau-de-change software exists, such as FXPlus, Money Exchanger Plus and CurrencyXchanger on Capterra, but none shows BSP or AMLC reporting. CTR and STR filing goes through the free AMLC portal (GoTRACS), so a product's value would be logging transactions, KYC records, the AML programme document and preparing the files, not the filing itself. Not checked: Philippine POS vendors for forex counters, and whether 247 RemitPlus is still sold.
first_check.reason: The duty is mandatory and enforced: BSP cancels registrations over AML lapses every year, and the M-Regulations were tightened in 2024-25. I found no affordable tool for small money changers. Several things hold the score down. Small changers rarely handle single cash deals over PHP 500k, so routine CTR filing is light. Filing is done on the free AMLC portal. Many operators are cash-only family businesses that are hard to reach and will pay little. Some BSP reporting forms may already be simple templates. A records, KYC and AML-programme pack plus a checklist of BSP reports is a workable MVP. It could be sold through the money changer associations, but the market is only a few thousand firms and willingness to pay is uncertain.

challenge_check.killer: None found. Partial weakeners: AMLC filing through GoTRACS is free; foreign bureau-de-change POS products (CurrencyXchanger, FXPlus, PSTForex) already do the transaction logging, though without BSP or AMLC output; most of the MSB count is probably remittance sub-agents and pawnshops on their principal's systems (my inference, not confirmed).
challenge_check.reason: I found nothing that kills it. The duty is current: BSP Circular 1206, approved by Monetary Board Resolution 1362 on 28 Nov 2024, consolidated the money service business rules into the M-Regulations, and the BSP keeps revoking registrations for AML failures. No product built for small Philippine money changers turned up. The tools that exist are enterprise AML (Tookitaki), foreign bureau-de-change POS (CurrencyXchanger, FXPlus, PSTForex, which targets Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and Thailand) and Mohur's 247 RemitPlus from 2016, with no sign it is still sold. The market is weaker than it looks. Filing through GoTRACS is free. Few small changers will see cash over PHP 500k in a day, so the work is mostly KYC records and STRs. The 7,357 MSB count includes remittance sub-agents, e-money issuers and pawnshops that use their principal's systems. I could not read the text of Circular 1206.
